cells.tense: You are in the place where direction is recognized, and you recognize it now.
cells.ask: Name one thing you are drawn toward, out loud, once. Then take the smallest step toward it today.
cells.core:
Two streams are meeting in you, and you can tell which one is yours. It doesn't come as an argument. It comes as direction, and you follow it because the following feels like remembering. What pulls you isn't a fantasy you invented. It's orientation, and it's working in you whether or not you put it into words. You notice what catches, you move with it, and the movement feels less like trying and more like agreeing.

What the pull wants now is not certainty and not a plan. It wants one clear step taken in its direction while the moment is fresh. You don't have to know where that step lands. Take it anyway.
cells.sheetLine: You can tell which way is yours. Take one step toward it.
cells.verb: choosing the one stream you'll flow with
cells.place: the place where you decide which direction to follow

cells.tense: You are pushing toward a version of this that hasn't arrived yet and can't be written in.
cells.ask: Pick the one connection that's actually here. Give it an ordinary hour today and let the others wait until they arrive on their own.
cells.core:
You've already decided how this should go, and you're living a few steps ahead of it. Every meeting becomes a chance to get there faster, and every delay reads as a failure you need to correct. The vision is real, but you're gripping it, and gripping a thing that hasn't arrived is how you miss the one that has.

What's here right now is one connection, not the shape of the whole thing. Give that one an ordinary hour, no outcome attached, and let the rest wait until they show up. The pull doesn't want your pushing. It wants your attention on what's actually in front of you.
cells.sheetLine: You're forcing a connection that's still forming. Let it arrive.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that closed behind you and never opened again.
cells.ask: Write down one thing you used to feel drawn toward. Then send one line to someone about it, before you've decided it's worth it.
cells.core:
Something in you used to draw toward things and it doesn't anymore, or you don't trust it to. A connection landed wrong, or a direction you followed turned out to be borrowed, and since then the pull has gone quiet. You can still describe what you think you want. You just can't feel it.

Forcing the feeling won't bring it back. Start by getting one thing out of your head and into the world — a sentence, a note, a small decision made with someone else's hands in it. Your own judgment comes back through contact, not through waiting. It returns slowly, and it returns from outside in.
cells.sheetLine: The pull hasn't gone. You've stopped trusting what it points at.
cells.verb: choosing the one stream you'll flow with

cells.tense: You are already steering toward something while saying the direction is still undecided.
cells.ask: Finish one thing you keep calling a draft. Show it to one person as yours, without the disclaimer about how rough it is.
cells.core:
The pull comes alive in you and it moves — you notice what catches your attention, you follow it, and the following feels like recognition. You don't force it and you don't explain it away. You just let it carry you forward.

But look at what you've actually been doing. The direction your attention keeps taking when nobody assigns it — that's not an accident, and it's not just practice. Somewhere in there is something you're following well, and you talk about it like it's still forming, still borrowed, still not quite the real thing. The direction is already yours. The only thing missing is the claim: one piece of it finished and shown as yours. That's not a ceremony. It's the difference between practicing and choosing.
cells.sheetLine: You're already following a direction. Stop calling it practice.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: that the person already knows which connection they want — plausible, but I can't see it from here, and the whole cell rests on it. A reader could say the choice isn't made yet, or that the direction felt borrowed; if so, the ask still works, because naming what you're drawn toward is useful whether or not it's already settled. Sentence serving the writer: any phrasing that makes the reader sound like they've already chosen and just won't admit it — that's a shape I like, not something I know.
